newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Relief seen in days for Russia gem industry.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Relief seen in days for Russia gem industry.

text.p: Russia will pass two documents in the next few days which would ease mounting pressure on its huge but troubled diamond industry, First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais said on Friday.
He said he stood by earlier predictions that a diamond export quota for the year would be finalised by the end of May and a long-delayed trade deal with De Beers signed by June 4 at the latest.

"What was said by me will be implemented," Chubais told a news conference. "In principal the decisions have been made, and will be signed soon," he said, adding there could be minor bureaucratic delays for both signings of a day or so.
Chubais' apparent determination to see the long-delayed documents passed will come as a relief to Russia's dominant diamond producer Almazy Rossii-Sakha (ARS).

ARS deputy vice president Lev Safonov told Itar-Tass news agency on Friday that rough gem exports from Russia had been practically blocked during the first five months of the year due to delays in outlining export quotas.

ARS suffered another blow in 1997 when De Beers sharply curtailed rough diamonds purchases from the company in response to Moscow's sluggish treatment of a draft trade deal submitted to the cabinet over seven months ago.
The last five months have been punctuated by a series of announcements and forecasts among Russian officials as to when the quota decree and gem trade deal might be passed.
But as part of President Boris Yeltsin's powerful reformist cabinet, Chubais' involvement appears to advance the process substantially.

"This is much more positive," said Des Kilalea, diamond analyst at Fleming Martin Securities in Johannesburg, referring to Chubais' remarks. "Because he is at the heart of the reformers, one feels he has the authority to say these things."

Kilalea said that while the signing of a trade deal between Russia and De Beers would be positive for the South African company, much depended on the terms of the agreement, which both sides have kept close to their chests.

In a statement in February ARS said Russia's position had been strengthened from earlier agreements in force until the end of 1996. But Kilalea said he doubted De Beers would cede too much ground to the Russian side.
"Obviously De Beers wants the deal, but I doubt they would give too much away," he said.

The key for De Beers was to control enough rough gem production in Russia, and of sufficiently high quality, to allow its customers to compete with Russia's own diamond cutters and polishers, who are supplied by ARS.
"If De Beers were unable to supply customers with rough diamonds at competitive prices, its customers would not be able to sell polished gems competitively either," Kilalea said.
This could put Russian diamond cutters and polishers at an advantage over their Western competitors, working against the South African gem giant, he added.
Chubais, on a visit to Russia's autonomous diamond-producing region of Yakutia earlier this month, said he wanted Russia's gem industry to have more autonomy in future.
But his desire to loosen the ties with De Beers, which controls the bulk of the world's diamond market, is unlikely to be realised any time soon, analysts said.

"Politically it is understandable that greater autonomy is important," said Kilalea. "But the real question is whether Russia can provide the tax incentives, skills and finances needed to create such an industry."
Russia accounts for about 20 percent of De Beers' Central Selling Organisation sales of rough diamonds. De Beers controls about 75 percent of the $4.5 billion annual world trade in uncut gems.
